coredata.dc:description: Streptococcus agalactiae is considered the main bacterial pathogen in cultured Nile tilapia. Formaldehyde-inactivated vaccines are the most accepted method for prevention and control of the disease. However, alternative inactivation methods for S. agalactiae vaccines have not been fully explored. Recently, we developed a hydrogen peroxide-inactivated vaccine against S. agalactiae with moderate efficacy, with the possibility to improve vaccine efficacy by adding adjuvants. The current study compared the efficacy of aluminum hydroxide and Freund's incomplete adjuvant (FIA) incorporated into a novel hydrogen peroxide-inactivated intraperitoneal vaccine against S. agalactiae for Nile tilapia fingerlings. The relative percentage survival (RPS) for aluminum hydroxide-adjuvanted vaccine (59.3%), and FIA-adjuvanted vaccine (77.8%) were higher than the vaccine without adjuvant (40.7%). In addition, fish immunized with aluminum hydroxide-adjuvanted vaccine had significantly higher levels of specific antibodies than control fish at 4 weeks post vaccination (wpv). Blood lymphocytes counts showed a decrease in vaccinated groups when compared to control fish, suggesting white cells migration to the tissues where antigen presentation is ongoing. Fish that received FIA-adjuvanted vaccine exhibited persistence of adjuvant deposits on intraperitoneal surfaces for at least 4 wpv that may be related to its superior performance compared to aluminum hydroxide adjuvanted vaccine, which did not evidence any type of deposit at any sampling times. The results observed in this study demonstrate that hydrogen peroxide-inactivated vaccine administered with either aluminum hydroxide or FIA induce optimal levels of protection, with a superior performance for FIA vaccine, which could be a good alternative to conventional formaldehyde-inactivated vaccines against S. agalactiae, due to its shorter manufacture time, and less toxicity.

ce:section.ce:para: Streptococcus agalactiae, a group B Streptococcus, is a Gram-positive bacterium [1], that can infect many freshwater, estuarine and marine fish species, particularly Nile tilapia Oreochromis niloticus [1,2]. Streptococcosis is characterized by septicemia and severe meningoencephalitis [1], and causes huge economic losses in tilapia culture [3], due to the high rates of infection and mortality that can reach up to 50–90% [1]. S. agalactiae has been responsible for several outbreaks of disease worldwide [4]. In Brazil, S. agalactiae infection occurs continuously, and is widely distributed geographically in the states of Paraná, São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Santa Catarina, Bahia, Ceará, Mato Grosso, Pernambuco, Goiás and Espírito Santo [5].

Sustainable aquaculture is not possible without disease prevention. Therefore, vaccination has become a significant prevention tool [6]. Vaccination is a widely accepted and effective method to control S. agalactiae infection and prevent mass mortality in tilapia [7]. Live attenuated vaccines have a great risk for reversion to virulence, thus spreading pathogenic bacteria into the environment [8]. For this reason, the use of inactivated or purified antigens is preferable.

Alternative methods for pathogen inactivation using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) have been standardized in recent years for mice vaccines against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas auruginosa [9], as well as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus [10], and rabies virus [11] with great success. Additionally, H2O2-inactivated vaccines have been tested in rhesus monkeys and mice against West Nile virus [12,13], reporting high efficacy and improvement of the adaptive immune response. H2O2 inactivation presents lower toxicity and preserves epitopes better than formaldehyde [9]. Recently, our research group compared the performance of a novel H2O2-inactivated vaccine against S. agalactiae in Nile tilapia showing equivalent efficacy to formaldehyde-inactivated vaccine and pH-manipulated vaccine [14]. During the vaccination trial, the vaccine proved to induce moderate efficacy against challenge using a homologous strain, despite no adjuvant was added to its formulation, suggesting that its efficacy can still be widely improved.

Inactivated vaccines are less immunogenic compared to live vaccines [15]. As a result, adjuvants have been indispensable for improvement of vaccine efficacy, by increasing the strength and length of protection [16]. Adjuvants increase the adaptive immune response [17–19] and can be classified as signal 1 and signal 2 facilitators [20]. Oily emulsions, also known as signal 1 facilitators, are the most commonly used [15]. Such adjuvants include the Freund's complete adjuvant (FCA), Freund's incomplete adjuvant (FIA) and Montanide [19], and have reported to potentiate vaccine efficacy when used in fish vaccines [21]. FIA is a water-oil (W/O) emulsion, that has proved to boost vaccine efficacy by stimulating higher antibody responses both humoral and mucosal when used in inactivated vaccines against S. agalactiae incorporated into the diet of red tilapia, Oreochromis sp. [22], and in polyvalent inactivated vaccines against Edwardsiella tarda and Vibrio anguillarum for Japanese flounder, Paralichthys olivaceus, evidencing high relative percent survival (RPS), of 70.9% and 67.4%, respectively [23]. Additionally, subunit vaccines against S. agalactiae, adjuvanted with FIA or Montanide, reported high RPS of 76.7% and 74.4%, respectively [24].

On the other hand, signal 2 facilitators activate cytokines and regulate costimulatory molecules during the antigen recognition phase, thus increasing the immune response during the vaccination period [19]. These facilitators include aluminum compounds such as aluminum hydroxide and aluminum phosphate [19]. So far, there are no studies relating to aluminum adjuvants to potentiate vaccines for tilapias. Previous studies involving vaccines against E. tarda in Japanese flounder with aluminum hydroxide or aluminum phosphate adjuvants revealed RPS of 53% and 69%, respectively and higher antibody titers for both vaccines when compared to the vaccine without adjuvant [25].

Therefore, the aim of the present study was to refine the efforts developed in our previous work [14] with a novel H2O2-inactivated vaccine against S. agalactiae for Nile tilapia, by enhancing its efficacy using adjuvants, and compare the efficacy of two adjuvants (FIA and aluminum hydroxide).

Streptococcus agalactiae strain (serotype Ib) used in this study was isolated from naturally infected Nile tilapia with clinical signs of streptococcosis in the northern region of Paraná State, Brazil [26]. The strain (SA43) was previously used to develop a H2O2-inactivated vaccine against S. agalactiae for Nile tilapia [14]. Bacteria were preserved in BHI broth (Kasvi, Brazil) containing 15% glycerol (v/v) in ultra-freezer at −80 °C until further use.

Nile tilapia fingerlings used during the study were obtained from a commercial fish farm, transported to the Sao Paulo State University facilities and placed in 250 L circular fiber tanks supplied with constant aeration, and continuous water flow (1 L/min). Before the experiment, fish were confirmed to be free of S. agalactiae infection by bacteriological analysis of brain, kidney and spleen samples in BHI plates. Fish were fed twice a day (8 a.m. and 4 p.m.) with commercial fish feed pellets (Laguna, Brazil: 36% crude protein) at 3% of body weight through the whole study. Fish were adapted for six weeks before the vaccination trial. Water quality parameters (temperature, dissolved oxygen and pH) were monitored daily by means of a multiparameter probe (U-50, Horiba, Japan). The water quality was kept within the optimal range for the species: temperature, 28.19 ± 0.54 °C, dissolved oxygen, 6.10 ± 1.70 mg/L and pH 7.20 ± 0.10 [27]. The present study was according to the ethical principles for animal experimentation of Brazilian laws of the National Council for the Control of Animal Experimentation of Brazil (CONCEA) and was approved by the Ethics Committee on Animal Use (CEUA) of Sao Paulo State University (protocol number 014772/19).

Following the acclimation period, 520 Nile tilapia fingerlings, mean weight 22.39 ± 1.71 g, and mean length 8.24 ± 0.16 cm, were randomly assigned into eight experimental groups in duplicate (20 fish per tank) with the exception of groups 1 and 2 that had a single replicate (20 fish per tank). Vaccine efficacy of a novel H2O2-inactivated immunogen against S. agalactiae was tested alone, alongside two types of adjuvants (FIA and aluminum hydroxide). Thus, two control groups for the adjuvants alone were included. Finally, a naïve group, without any handling, and two control groups, one non-vaccinated and non-challenged and the second non-vaccinated and challenged were included. Distribution was as it follows: Group 1: naïve; Group 2: non-vaccinated, non-challenged; Group 3: non-vaccinated and challenged; Group 4: aluminum hydroxide; Group 5: FIA; Group 6: H2O2-vaccine; Group 7: H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and Group 8: H2O2-vaccine + FIA. Fish were vaccinated and four weeks later were challenged with the lethal dose 50% (LD50-21d) of a homologous S. agalactiae strain. Additionally, two extra replicates, without bacterial challenge, were added (20 fish per tank) for groups 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 for determination of anti-S. agalactiae IgM antibodies, hematological parameters, respiratory burst activity, serum total proteins, albumin, globulin, albumin/globulin ratio and evaluation of intra-abdominal lesions at 2 and 4 weeks post-vaccination (wpv) (seven fish per period). Vaccine was administered by intraperitoneal (IP) injection (0.1 mL). Prior to vaccination, fish were anesthetized by immersion in benzocaine (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, USA) solution (100 mg/L) [28]. After injection, all fish were returned to their tanks, and water flow was interrupted. During this period, water temperature was kept at 28 °C using heaters and water quality parameters were maintained at optimal conditions with daily water changes (up to 10%).

Twenty-eight days post-vaccination, challenged groups (3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8) were anesthetized as described above and injected IP with 0.1 mL of a homologous S. agalactiae strain and monitored daily for clinical signs and mortality for 21 days. Dead and moribund fish were removed twice a day before feeding and bacterial samples were aseptically obtained from brain, head kidney, liver and spleen to confirm S. agalactiae as the cause of dead. Vaccine efficacy was assessed by means of the relative percentage of survival (RPS), calculated according to formula: RPS = [1 − (% mortality in vaccinated fish/% mortality in control fish)] × 100 [29].

Previously, a method to inactivate S. agalactiae with H2O2 was validated for vaccine formulation for Nile tilapia [14]. Briefly, S. agalactiae colonies were incubated in several 300 mL BHI broth in an incubator shaker (C24 Classic Series, New Brunswick Scientific, New Jersey, USA) at 150 rpm, 28 °C, for 72 h. A 30% stock solution of H2O2 (Labsynth, Brazil) was sterilized by membrane filtration and kept in a dark sealed container. H2O2 was added to the bacterial suspension, in order to obtain a final concentration of 5%, previously determined as the optimal dose required to effectively inactivate S. agalactiae [14]. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C for 6 h. Then, the bacteria were washed three times with PBS by centrifugation at 10.000g, for 10 min, at 4 °C. The bacterial number was adjusted by spectrophotometry at an optical density (OD540nm = 1.260) (SP-22, Biospectro, Brazil) and confirmed by plate count (2.6 × 1010 CFU/mL), prior to inactivation. Antigen dose was chosen based on a previous study [14]. In order to confirm inactivation, 100 μl of the inoculum was streaked onto BHI plates and incubated at 28 °C, for 72 h. Finally, the vaccine was stored at 4 °C until use.

Vaccine mixture was prepared at twice the concentration stated above (5.2 × 1010 CFU/mL), so when diluted with the adjuvant the amount of antigen was equal between groups that received the vaccine alone or the adjuvanted vaccines. Then, the vaccine was emulsified with FIA (Sigma-Aldrich F5506, St. Louis, USA) at a ratio of 1:1 by vortexing at maximum speed for 15 min in sterilized Falcon tubes filled at its maximum capacity to avoid air entrance [30]. Finally, the vaccine was stored at 4 °C until vaccination.

ce:section.ce:section-title: H2O2-inactivated S. agalactiae + aluminum hydroxide vaccine
ce:section.ce:para: Vaccine mixture was prepared as stated in Section 2.4.2 at a concentration of 5.2 × 1010 CFU/mL. Then, the vaccine was mixed with a 0.5% sterile aluminum hydroxide solution (w/v) (Sigma-Aldrich, 239186, St. Louis, USA) at a 1:1 ratio and followed the same procedure described for the FIA vaccine. Finally, the vaccine was stored at 4 °C until vaccination.

A homologous S. agalactiae strain was used for the challenge. Frozen bacterial stocks were subcultured onto BHI agar at 28 °C for 48–72 h. Then, colonies were selected and inoculated into 300 mL of BHI broth. Next, bacteria were washed twice with sterile PBS by centrifugation at 10.000g, for 10min, at 4 °C. The cell pellet was re-suspended in PBS and adjusted to an OD540nm = 0.575 and confirmed as a dose of 1.7 × 106 CFU/mL, the dose was based on a lethal dose 50% (LD50-21d) calculated previously by testing several bacterial dilutions in groups of 10 fish from the same batch (data not shown).

Non-challenged replicates from groups non-vaccinated (Group 2), aluminum hydroxide, FIA, H2O2-vaccine, H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were used for blood sampling at 2 and 4 wpv, collected by caudal venipuncture (seven fish previously anesthetized from each group) with 1 mL syringes with 26-G needles containing 10% EDTA (Vetec, RJ, Brazil) or without anticoagulant. A total of seven fish previously anesthetized from each group were used for hematological parameters, respiratory burst activity, serum total proteins, albumin, globulin, and albumin/globulin ratio, while only five from the total seven were used for determination of IgM antibody anti-S. agalactiae. Blood without anticoagulant was transferred to microtubes, allowed to clot for 30 min at room temperature and later centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 5 min and stored at −80 °C until further analysis (Anti-S. agalactiae IgM antibodies, serum total proteins, albumin, and globulin). Blood with EDTA was used immediately for hematological analysis and determination of respiratory burst activity.

The sera were subjected to indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) according to previous methodologies [14,31] using a mouse anti-tilapia IgM monoclonal antibody (Aquatic Diagnostics Ltd, Stirling, UK), a peroxidase conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, A4416, St. Louis, USA) and a TMB Substrate (Tetramethylbenzidine) (Sigma-Aldrich, TA4444, St. Louis, USA).

The total red blood cell (RBC, 106 cells/μL) counts were performed in a Neubauer chamber under light microscopy. Hematocrit (Htc %) evaluation followed the microhematocrit method [32]. Hemoglobin concentration (g/dL) was determined using a commercial kit (Labtest, Minas Gerais, Brazil) according to the cyanometahemoglobin method [33]. Hematimetric indexes: mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) were also assessed [34]. Additionally, blood smears were stained with rapid panoptic staining for total thrombocyte, total leukocyte and differential leukocyte counts by light microscopy using an indirect method [35].

The production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was measured by the reduction of nitro blue tetrazolium (NBT) according to a previous methodology reported by Cueva-Quiroz et al. [36], using a NBT solution (Sigma-Aldrich, N5514, St. Louis, USA) and N, N- dimethylformamide (DMF) (Sigma-Aldrich, D4551, St. Louis, USA).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of serum total proteins, albumin and globulin
ce:section.ce:para: Serum total proteins and albumin were determined by Biuret and bromocresol method, respectively, by using a commercial kit (Labtest, Minas Gerais, Brazil), following the manufacturer's instructions. The globulin content was estimated by subtracting the albumin content from total protein content.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Evaluation of intra-abdominal lesions after vaccination
ce:section.ce:para: Five fish per group used for blood collection were euthanized by overdose in benzocaine solution and used for evaluation of intra-abdominal lessons at 2 and 4 wpv. The abdominal cavity was exposed by excising the left belly flap in order to observe adhesions, granulomas, or adjuvant deposits in the internal organs such as liver, spleen, intestine, pyloric caeca, and stomach. The adhesions were classified according to Midtlyng scale [37]. The evaluation was performed by one investigator, who was not aware of the experimental groups identity.

All data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 7 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, USA) First, data were tested for normality (Shapiro-Wilk test). One-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test or Kruskal Wallis with Dunn's post-test were used to identify statistical differences between experimental groups and Student's t-test or Mann Whitney U test were conducted to determine significant differences between sampling times. Data were expressed as mean ± SEM. The significance level was defined as P < 0.05. The survival curves were analyzed by Kaplan-Meier analysis and log rank test. Survival values were adjusted for multiple comparisons by means of the Bonferroni corrected threshold. We counted the number of comparisons that we pretended to perform, and call this value K (K = 6). Then, we adjusted the level of significance by dividing, the family-wise level (0.05) by 6, this obtaining a new P value = 0.0083.

No fish died during the vaccination period (four weeks). Naïve and non-vaccinated, non-challenged groups did not evidence any clinical sign during the challenge period. Regarding the challenged groups, mortality started at the 6th, 5th and 2nd day after challenge in groups non-vaccinated, aluminum hydroxide and FIA, respectively, and at 5th day in groups H2O2-vaccine and H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide. Finally, in the H2O2-vaccine + FIA group mortality started at the 4th day after bacterial challenge. Clinical signs in the challenged fish from groups that did not received any type of vaccine included changes in skin coloration, exophthalmia, corneal opacity, anorexia, lethargy and erratic swimming in circles. Vaccinated groups mostly evidenced anorexia, lethargy and dark skin coloration.

The survival percentage of groups naïve; non-vaccinated, non-challenged; and non-vaccinated, challenged were 100%, 100% and 32.5%. On the other hand, fish injected with adjuvants alone, both, aluminum hydroxide and FIA achieved a survival percentage of 27.5% and 22.5%. Finally, vaccinated groups, either H2O2-vaccine, H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide, and H2O2-vaccine + FIA reached 60%, 72.5% and 85% of survival percentage, respectively. The data displayed higher survival for vaccinated groups when compared to group non-vaccinated, non-challenged (Group 3). Notwithstanding, there was no statistical difference in survival between H2O2-vaccine group and non-vaccinated challenged group. Conversely, vaccinated groups H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA did reveal significantly higher survival (p < 0.05). No statistical difference in the percentage of survival was found between vaccinated groups (Fig. 1 ). Hence, the immune protective efficacies, in terms of RPS, of groups H2O2-vaccine, H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide, and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were 40.7%, 59.3% and 77.8%, respectively.

The ELISA test showed that anti-S. agalactiae IgM antibodies were not significantly different (P > 0.05) between vaccinated groups and non-vaccinated (Group 2) at 2 wpv (Fig. 2 ). Nevertheless, IgM antibodies of group H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide were significantly higher than those determined for group non-vaccinated (Group 3) at 4 wpv. Likewise, the results showed that anti S. agalactiae IgM antibodies of groups aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine were significantly higher at 2 wpv when compared to those at wpv.

The erythrogram did not show significant differences between vaccinated groups and control groups, including adjuvants alone and non-vaccinated group (Group 2) (Table 1 ). There were significant higher values (P < 0.05) in group H2O2-vaccine when compared to group H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide for hemoglobin levels and group FIA was significantly higher than H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide for MCHC at 2 wpv. Hemoglobin values of groups FIA, H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA, and MCHC values of groups non-vaccinated and H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide at 2 wpv were significantly lower compared to those at 4 wpv. Additionally, MCV values in group H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide were significantly higher at 2 wpv than at 4 wpv.

The leukogram (Fig. 3 ) revealed that total lymphocyte numbers of groups FIA, H2O2-vaccine, H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide, and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were significantly lower (P < 0.05) than non-vaccinated group at 2 wpv. In addition, the study showed significantly higher values for total leukocytes in aluminum hydroxide group when compared to group H2O2-vaccine, higher values in group non-vaccinated (Group 2) when compared to groups FIA, H2O2-vaccine, H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA for lymphocytes, higher values in group H2O2-vaccine when compared to groups H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA for monocytes at 2 wpv.

Furthermore, significantly higher values in group H2O2-vaccine compared to group non-vaccinated for total granulocytes and monocytes, significantly higher values in group aluminum hydroxide when compared to groups FIA and H2O2-vaccine + FIA for total leukocytes, higher values in group H2O2-vaccine when compared to groups non-vaccinated, FIA, H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA for granulocytes, higher values in group aluminum hydroxide when compared to groups H2O2-vaccine and H2O2-vaccine + FIA for lymphocytes and higher values in group H2O2-vaccine when compared to the others groups for monocytes at 4 wpv. Analysis of the two sampling times showed that total leukocyte and lymphocyte values of groups H2O2-vaccine and H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide at 2 wpv were significantly lower compared to those at 4 wpv; total granulocyte values of groups H2O2-vaccine and H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide at 2 wpv were significantly lower and higher, respectively, when compared to those at 4 wpv; total monocyte values of groups non-vaccinated, aluminum hydroxide, FIA, H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA at 2 wpv were significantly lower than at 4 wpv. Finally, thrombocytes values of groups non-vaccinated, aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were higher at 2 wpv when compared to those at 4 wpv.

The respiratory burst activity evidenced no significant differences (P > 0.05) between vaccinated groups and non-vaccinated group (Group 2) at 2 wpv (Fig. 4 ). However, burst respiratory activity was significantly higher in groups non-vaccinated, aluminum hydroxide, H2O2-vaccine and H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide compared to FIA and H2O2-vaccine + FIA at 4 wpv. Finally, a significant decrease was observed in groups FIA and H2O2-vaccine + FIA at 4 wpv compared to values observed at 2 wpv.

The serum total proteins values in aluminum hydroxide group were significantly higher than group H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide at 2 wpv, though the situation was reversed at 4 wpv (Table 2 ). Moreover, aluminum hydroxide group had significantly higher values at 2 wpv than at 4 wpv (P < 0.05). Albumin levels were significantly lower (P < 0.05) in group H2O2-vaccine than groups H2O2-vaccine + FIA and non-vaccinated (Group 2), and significantly lower in group FIA compared to group H2O2-vaccine + FIA at 2 wpv. On the other hand, no differences were identified at 4 wpv. Albumin levels showed a significant increase between 2 and 4 wpv for group H2O2-vaccine, and a significant decrease for group H2O2-vaccine + FIA. Globulin levels were significantly lower (P < 0.05) at 2 wpv in group non-vaccinated compared to group aluminum hydroxide, and at 4 wpv were significantly lower in group aluminum hydroxide compared to group H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide. Globulins levels were significantly higher in group non-vaccinated at 4 wpv than at 2 wpv. Albumin: globulin ratio was significantly lower (P < 0.05) in group H2O2-vaccine when compared to non-vaccinated and H2O2-vaccine + FIA at 2 wpv. In addition, albumin/globulin ratio was significantly higher at 2 wpv than at 4 wpv (P < 0.05) for groups non-vaccinated, and H2O2-vaccine + FIA. However, H2O2-vaccine values increased significantly between 2 and 4 wpv.

Necropsy observations of the abdominal cavity revealed adjuvant deposits around the posterior esophagus, liver, gallbladder and intestine at 2 and 4 wpv in groups FIA and H2O2-vaccine + FIA. Adjuvant deposits ranging in size from 1 to 5 mm showed whitish coloration, oily consistency and oval or round shape. Furthermore, mild adhesions were seen between internal organs and the abdominal wall. No adjuvant deposits nor adhesions were seen in groups aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide (Fig. 5 ).

The present study tested the efficacy of an experimental H2O2-inactivated vaccine against S. agalactiae with two different adjuvants (FIA and aluminum hydroxide). Most fish vaccination studies use formaldehyde for bacterial inactivation [38, 39, 40]. Despite formaldehyde being a strong inactivating agent, it can have negative effects on physical and chemical characteristics of superficial antigens and on the immune response [10] by modifying the integrity of epitopes, affecting antigenic determinants on the cell wall [9]. Furthermore, formaldehyde inactivated vaccines do not always show high efficacy [37].

The percentage of survival of the two vaccinated and adjuvanted groups H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA showed high values over 70% (72.5% and 85%, respectively), higher than group H2O2-vaccine (60%), and were significantly higher than non-vaccinated group, verifying that the inclusion of adjuvants improved the response to vaccination. Previous results in Japanese flounder vaccinated against E. tarda using aluminum hydroxide and FIA as adjuvants showed percentages of survival of 55% and 82%, respectively, higher than the group vaccinated, but without adjuvants (37%) [25]. The RPS of H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were considered optimal (59.3% and 77.8%, respectively) and were considerably higher than the vaccine without adjuvants (40.7%). Optimal RPS are considered to be higher than or equal to 60% [41]. Studies in rainbow trout Oncorynchus mykiss immunized with a formaldehyde-inactivated vaccine against S. iniae using FCA also showed high RPS values (73.9–95%) [42]. Moreover, studies in Japanese flounder vaccinated against E. tarda using FIA and aluminum hydroxide, showed RPS values of 81.0% and 53%, respectively, higher than the vaccinated group without adjuvant (34%) [25]. Low toxicity and high immunoestimulant effect of FIA during vaccination trials [18], could explain the higher RPS. Aluminum hydroxide adjuvanted vaccines have proven to be ineffective when used in diseases where a cellular response predominates [18], which could be explained because of a lower depot effect in aluminum adjuvants than oil emulsions [18].

The H2O2-inactivated vaccine proved to be highly effective when administered with both adjuvants. Previous results using this same methodology for inactivation of S. agalactiae in a novel experimental vaccine without adjuvants in Nile Tilapia [14] showed a moderate efficacy (RPS: 46.6%), comparable to the one obtained in the present study by the group administrated with the vaccine alone (RPS: 40.7%). Although, higher antigen doses were administered in the present study (2.6 × 1010 CFU/mL), compared to our previous study [14] where 1.54 × 109 CFU/mL were used, vaccine protection remained the same, suggesting that higher antigen doses do not increase vaccine efficacy for this vaccine type.

The anti-S. agalactiae IgM antibodies showed no major differences between unvaccinated or vaccinated groups at 2 wpv, however significant differences were detected at 4 wpv. Antibody titers are a measure of protective immunity for fish vaccines and can be considered as suboptimal or protective according to correlate of protection [43]. Antibody levels in H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide group were significantly higher than non-vaccinated group (Group 2) at 4 wpv. These values confirm the humoral response stimulation of aluminum hydroxide [18]. On the other hand, the values of RPS were moderate (59.3%), which could indicate that the immune humoral response was not high enough to induce an effective protection, probably because of a survival intracellular mechanism of S. agalactiae [44]. Even though group H2O2-vaccine + FIA did not show significant differences in antibody levels at 4 wpv, it evidenced an undoubtedly higher efficacy, perhaps due to an improvement of the cellular response due to the FIA [19] above the humoral response. Antibody levels in group H2O2-vaccine showed a decrease at 4 wpv when compared to 2 wpv, which could suggest that the vaccine without adjuvant was not able to maintain the antibody levels until the 4th week. The duration of the vaccine protection depends upon several factors, including water temperature, as well as the vaccination procedure, and characteristics of the vaccine such as type: inactivated or attenuated, use of adjuvants, among others [45].

Hematological parameters have been considered as important indicators of fish health [46]. The hematological values showed significantly higher hemoglobin at 2 wpv in group H2O2-vaccine compared to group H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide, which could be related to fish physiological changes during the study [47].

Lymphocytes values in groups FIA, H2O2-vaccine, H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were lower than group non-vaccinated at 2 wpv. The decrease of total lymphocytes and leukocytes could be explained due to migration of the immune cells to the tissues where the antigen presentation is ongoing [48]. Monocyte counts of groups H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + FIA were significantly higher than H2O2-vaccine group at 2 wpv, and total leukocyte counts in group aluminum hydroxide were significantly higher than group H2O2-vaccine + FIA at 4 wpv. In a study with a polyvalent vaccine, monocytes values after 7 days post-vaccination, and neutrophils values after 7 and 21 days post-vaccination were higher in non-vaccinated Nile tilapia, compared to fish that were vaccinated against Aeromonas hydrophila, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterococcus durans [49]. In contrast, neutrophil decreased 30 days after vaccination against Aeromonas bestiarum in carps [50]. The higher lymphocyte counts at 4 wpv in group aluminum hydroxide compared to groups H2O2-vaccine and H2O2-vaccine + FIA could be explained due to migration of lymphocytes to lymphoid organs in vaccinated groups [48]. Finally, thrombocytes values in group H2O2-vaccine + FIA decreased at 4 wpv compared to those at 2 wpv, in contrast to reports in Nile tilapias after polyvalent immunization [49].

The respiratory burst activity is an oxygen-dependent reaction used by phagocytes to kill pathogens and is an indicator of killing activity of phagocytic cells [51]. The study showed higher values of respiratory burst activity at 4 wpv in groups non-vaccinated (Group 2), aluminum hydroxide, H2O2-vaccine and H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide compared to groups FIA and H2O2-vaccine + FIA. Contrasting our results, values of respiratory burst activity were significantly higher at 21 and 42 days post-vaccination compared to control group in Labeo rohita vaccinated against A. hydrophila with antigen adsorbed calcium phosphate nanoparticles [52].

Serum protein levels were higher in group aluminum hydroxide compared to group H2O2- vaccine + aluminum hydroxide at 2 wpv. However, the values of proteins were higher in group H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide compared to group aluminum hydroxide at 4 wpv, which could be due to the increase of total proteins related to stimulation of the immune response. Some adjuvants provide co-stimulatory signals during the antigen recognition phase, activating the production of different proteins [19].

Serum albumin levels and albumin: globulin ratio did not show significant differences at 2 wpv, except for fish that received the H2O2-vaccine, where the values were lower than non-vaccinated fish. These results are contrary to those described in Epinephelus bruneus vaccinated against Vibrio harveyi which showed higher levels for these parameters in vaccinated groups [53]. Low albumin: globulin ratio could be related to an increase in globulin levels, perhaps caused by the increase of immunoglobulins, which are important proteins to maintain a healthy immune system [54]. Serum globulin levels in different groups at 2 wpv were higher for the aluminum hydroxide group compared to non-vaccinated fish, which could be attributed to a potent adjuvant reaction. At 4 wpv, group H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide exhibited higher serum globulin compared to group aluminum hydroxide, which could mean an increase in humoral response, a characteristic of this particular adjuvant [18].

During evaluation of intra-abdominal lessons, intraperitoneal deposits were not observed in fish from groups aluminum hydroxide and H2O2-vaccine + aluminum hydroxide or H2O2- vaccine alone. The dose of the adjuvant use in the present study was 1000 μg. In contrast, toxicity assays of aluminum hydroxide in Paralichthys olivaceus revealed adjuvant deposits when used at doses of 500, 1600 and 5000 μg at 8 and 15 days post-injection [55]. Another study relating adverse effects of adjuvants in Scophthalmus maximus, showed mild to moderate adhesions in abdominal cavity caused by aluminum hydroxide [56]. Therefore, the deposit effect is likely to be temporary in aluminum-adjuvanted vaccines. Groups FIA and H2O2-vaccine + FIA revealed round deposits in the abdominal cavity and mild adhesions between internal organs and the abdominal wall at 2 and 4 wpv. Similar results were described in internal organs of Japanese flounder at the 15th day post-injection using oily adjuvants, manifested as whitish deposits in the liver and intestine, but without adhesions [55]. In addition, studies about adverse effects of adjuvants in Scophthalmus maximus, showed severe adhesions in abdominal cavity using oily adjuvants [56]. Oil-based adjuvants have shown a persistence of antigen at the injection site, which is a prerequisite for long-term protection, by increasing the exposure time of the antigen to the immune system [18]. The fact that adjuvant deposits persisted on intraperitoneal surfaces for at least four weeks, could be related to the strong protection induced by the vaccine with FIA.

The results observed in this study are promising on the use of H2O2 as an alternative methodology to conventional formaldehyde bacterial inactivation. In addition, this type of vaccine proved to be highly effective when administered with two of the most common adjuvants used in aquaculture. Future studies should focus on improving the vaccine efficacy.
